title: Antiparasitic Drugs
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Parasitic Infections and Antiparasitic Therapy
headings.content: Parasitic infections represent a significant global health challenge, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions such as Nigeria, where environmental factors favor the proliferation of various parasites. These infections can be classified broadly into protozoa (single-celled organisms) and helminths (multicellular worms), alongside ectoparasites that inhabit the skin. Antiparasitic drugs are pharmacological agents designed to eradicate or inhibit the multiplication of these parasites with minimal host toxicity. Unlike bacteria, parasites are eukaryotic organisms, which makes finding unique drug targets that do not harm human host cells a complex pharmacological hurdle. Successful antiparasitic therapy relies on understanding the life cycle of the invading organism, the specific drug's mechanism of action, and patient-specific variables such as immune status and liver function, which metabolizes many of these compounds. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice and professional board examinations, mastering antiparasitic medications is essential for providing effective, evidence-based care. Nurses must recognize the clinical manifestations of diverse parasitic infestations, anticipate pharmacological interventions, and monitor patients closely for therapeutic efficacy and adverse reactions. Furthermore, because many parasitic infections are linked to poor sanitation, contaminated water supplies, and overcrowding, comprehensive nursing care extends beyond medication administration to include public health education, promotion of hygiene, and community-level prevention strategies that break the transmission cycle.

headings.title: Anthelmintics: Classification, Mechanism of Action, and Nursing Care
headings.content: Anthelmintics are specialized medications used to treat infections caused by parasitic worms, known as helminths, which include nematodes (roundworms), cestodes (tapeworms), and trematodes (flukes). Common examples frequently encountered in clinical settings include albendazole, mebendazole, ivermectin, and praziquantel. These drugs operate via diverse mechanisms: benzimidazoles like albendazole inhibit microtubule synthesis in the parasite, disrupting its glucose uptake and depleting its glycogen stores until it dies of starvation. Ivermectin binds selectively to glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells, causing increased permeability, hyperpolarization, paralysis, and death of the parasite. Praziquantel increases the cell membrane permeability of trematodes and cestodes to calcium ions, resulting in rapid contraction, paralysis, and subsequent destruction by the host immune system. Nursing care for patients receiving anthelmintics requires careful pre-treatment assessment, including confirmation of the specific parasite via stool microscopy. Nurses must monitor for gastrointestinal side effects such as abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea, which often occur as the dying worms are expelled from the gastrointestinal tract. In patients with heavy parasite loads, dying worms can trigger acute inflammatory responses or allergic reactions, necessitating the administration of concurrent corticosteroids or antihistamines as prescribed. Nurses must also educate patients on proper hand hygiene, washing raw fruits and vegetables, and treating all household members simultaneously to prevent reinfection.

headings.title: Antimalarial Agents: Types, Pharmacodynamics, and Patient Monitoring
headings.content: Malaria remains a devastating vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae) and transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. Antimalarial agents are categorized based on their specific phase in the parasite's life cycle and clinical objective, encompassing chemoprophylaxis, acute attack treatment, and prevention of relapse. Major drug classes include artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), quinolines (such as chloroquine, quinine, and mefloquine), and antifolates. Artemisinins, recommended by the World Health Organization as first-line treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, work by producing free radicals through the interaction of their endoperoxide bridge with intra-parasitic iron, damaging parasite proteins and membranes. Chloroquine acts by blocking heme detoxification within the parasite, leading to a toxic buildup of free heme that destroys the organism. Pharmacodynamic monitoring is vital because many antimalarial drugs have narrow therapeutic indices. For instance, quinine can cause cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, visual disturbances) and severe hypoglycemia, while chloroquine requires baseline and periodic ophthalmologic assessments during long-term use due to the risk of irreversible retinal damage. Nurses play a critical role in observing for treatment failure, assessing for severe malaria symptoms (like cerebral malaria or severe anemia), and educating patients on completing the full course of medication even after symptoms subside to prevent resistance and recurrence.

headings.title: Antiprotozoal Drugs: Treatment of Amebiasis, Giardiasis, and Trichomoniasis
headings.content: Protozoal infections such as amebiasis (caused by Entamoeba histolytica), giardiasis (caused by Giardia lamblia), and trichomoniasis (caused by Trichomonas vaginalis) affect millions globally, particularly in areas with compromised water sanitation. The mainstay pharmacological agent for treating these protozoal infestations is metronidazole, alongside alternatives like tinidazole and nitazoxanide. Metronidazole is a prodrug that enters the protozoal cell by passive diffusion and is activated through reduction of its nitro group by ferredoxin-like electron transport proteins found strictly in anaerobic organisms. Once activated, metronidazole forms cytotoxic reactive intermediates that bind to microbial DNA, causing strand breakage, helical destabilization, and ultimately cell death. Because these pathogens inhabit different body sites—such as the intestinal lumen, liver tissue (amebic liver abscesses), or urogenital tract—treatment regimens may combine luminal amebicides (like paromomycin) with systemic tissue amebicides (like metronidazole) to ensure complete eradication. Nursing care for patients on metronidazole includes strict education on avoiding alcohol consumption during treatment and for at least three days post-therapy, as the drug induces a severe disulfiram-like reaction characterized by flushing, severe nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, and hypotension. Nurses should also monitor for common adverse effects such as a metallic taste in the mouth, dark-colored urine, peripheral neuropathy, and gastrointestinal upset, while ensuring partner treatment in cases of sexually transmitted trichomoniasis to prevent ping-pong infections.

headings.title: Ectoparasiticides: Management of Scabies and Pediculosis
headings.content: Ectoparasiticides are topical and systemic medications utilized to manage infestations of the skin and hair by external parasites, most notably scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei) and pediculosis (lice, including head, body, and pubic lice). Common topical agents include permethrin (a synthetic pyrethroid), malathion, benzyl alcohol, and ivermectin lotion. Permethrin acts by disrupting the voltage-gated sodium channels in the nerve cell membranes of arthropods, leading to delayed repolarization, paralysis, and death of the parasite and its ova. Ivermectin can also be administered orally for resistant cases of scabies or pediculosis. Nursing management in ectoparasitic infestations centers on meticulous application instructions and stringent environmental control to prevent re-infestation. For topical creams like permethrin, nurses must instruct patients to apply the cream thoroughly from the neck down to the soles of the feet (paying special attention to skin folds, webbing between fingers and toes, and under fingernails) and leave it on for the prescribed duration (typically 8 to 14 hours) before washing it off thoroughly. Environmental measures are equally critical: all bed linens, towels, and clothing used within the preceding 72 hours must be machine-washed in hot water and dried on high heat, or sealed in plastic bags for two weeks if non-washable. Furthermore, nurses should perform contact tracing, screen household members and close personal contacts simultaneously, and educate patients that intense pruritus may persist for several weeks after successful parasite eradication due to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens.

headings.title: General Adverse Effects and Drug Interactions of Antiparasitic Medications
headings.content: Antiparasitic medications span diverse chemical classes, and consequently, they carry a wide array of general adverse effects and complex drug interactions that nurses must anticipate and manage. Gastrointestinal distress—including nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea—is nearly ubiquitous across this pharmacological category, often exacerbated by the death of parasites within the GI tract. Many antiparasitic agents are metabolized hepatically through the cytochrome P450 enzyme system, predisposing them to significant drug-drug interactions. For instance, medications like albendazole and praziquantel can have their plasma concentrations altered when co-administered with CYP450 inducers (such as rifampin or anticonvulsants) or inhibitors (such as cimetidine). Additionally, several antimalarials and antiparasitics (like chloroquine, quinine, and pentamidine) are notorious for causing cardiac toxicities, specifically QT interval prolongation and potential fatal arrhythmias, making baseline electrocardiograms (ECGs) crucial when combining them with other QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., antipsychotics or macrolide antibiotics). Bone marrow suppression, neurotoxicity (manifesting as dizziness, ataxia, or peripheral neuropathy), and hepatotoxicity are also serious systemic adverse effects associated with prolonged or high-dose therapy. Nurses must review the patient's comprehensive medication reconciliation list, assess baseline liver and renal function laboratory values, and monitor vital signs meticulously to catch early signs of systemic toxicity or adverse drug interactions before they result in organ failure.

headings.title: Nursing Responsibilities and Patient Education for Safe Administration
headings.content: Safe administration of antiparasitic medications requires rigorous nursing responsibilities centered on accurate assessment, safe dosage calculation, vigilant patient monitoring, and comprehensive education. Prior to initiating therapy, nurses must obtain a thorough baseline health history, including pregnancy and lactation status (as many antiparasitic drugs are teratogenic), history of hepatic or renal impairment, and known drug allergies. Dosage calculations for pediatric patients must be meticulously verified against weight-based parameters (mg/kg) to prevent toxicity or under-dosing that could foster drug resistance. During administration, nurses should ensure medications are taken with food or on an empty stomach precisely as prescribed to optimize absorption and minimize gastrointestinal upset. Patient education is the cornerstone of successful antiparasitic regimens. Nurses must emphasize the absolute necessity of completing the entire prescribed course of medication, even if symptoms resolve rapidly, to eradicate the parasite fully and prevent relapses or drug-resistant strains. Education must also incorporate practical prevention strategies: teaching proper handwashing techniques, safe drinking water practices (such as boiling or filtering), thorough washing and cooking of meat and vegetables, proper sanitation and latrine usage, and the simultaneous treatment of sexual partners or household contacts when indicated. Finally, nurses should schedule appropriate follow-up diagnostic testing, such as repeat stool microscopy or blood smears, to confirm microbiological cure and therapeutic success.
